elements.element: Vendor has an express duty to defend Customer and its affiliates.
elements.evidence: Section 6.3(a)(i) now reads "The Servicer will defend and indemnify the Issuer and its Affiliates, the Owner Trustee and the Indenture Trustee ..." and (a)(ii) "The Marketing Agent will defend and indemnify the Indemnified Persons"; the duty to defend is mandatory ("will defend") and extends to the Issuer's Affiliates, who are folded into the "Indemnified Person" definition set in (a)(i).

elements.element: Vendor indemnifies Customer and its affiliates against third-party claims.
elements.evidence: Both (a)(i) and (a)(ii) indemnify the Indemnified Persons (now including the Issuer and its Affiliates) for "all fees, expenses, losses, claims, actions, suits, damages and liabilities (including reasonable legal fees and expenses)", which is broader than, and therefore captures, third-party claims; the new limb (C) is expressly framed as "any claim that any services or deliverables ... infringe".

elements.element: Vendor indemnity covers claims that Services or Deliverables infringe intellectual property rights.
elements.evidence: New paragraph: "(C) any claim that any services or deliverables it provides under the Transaction Documents infringe or misappropriate any intellectual property right."

elements.element: Vendor indemnity covers Vendor's breach of applicable law.
elements.evidence: New paragraph limb "(A) its violation of applicable Law", applicable to both the Servicer and the Marketing Agent (i.e., both Cellco capacities).

elements.element: Vendor indemnity covers a data breach caused by Vendor.
elements.evidence: New paragraph limb "(B) any unauthorized access to or disclosure of Obligor data or Receivable Files caused by it (including the Servicer in its capacity as Custodian)" — a Vendor-caused data breach trigger keyed to the categories of Issuer-side data Cellco actually holds.

elements.element: Vendor indemnity covers Vendor's gross negligence and wilful misconduct.
elements.evidence: Retained in (a)(i) and (a)(ii): "resulting from the Servicer's (including in its capacity as Custodian) willful misconduct, bad faith or gross negligence in performing its obligations under the Transaction Documents" (and the parallel Marketing Agent limb).

elements.element: The indemnification procedure requires notice of a claim.
elements.evidence: Section 6.3(b) retained: the Indemnified Person will "promptly notify the Servicer or the Marketing Agent, as applicable, of the Proceeding", with a non-prejudice proviso.

elements.element: The indemnification procedure allocates control of the defence.
elements.evidence: Retained: "The Servicer or the Marketing Agent, as applicable, may participate in and assume the defense and settlement of a Proceeding at its expense", followed by the counsel-standard and conflict-of-interest mechanics governing assumed defence — control is allocated (electively to the indemnitor, with separate-counsel protection for the Indemnified Person).

elements.element: The indemnification procedure requires reasonable cooperation.
elements.evidence: Added sentence in the Proceedings mechanics: "The Indemnified Person will provide reasonable cooperation in the defense of the Proceeding."

elements.element: Customer indemnity is limited to Customer-provided content and Customer's breach of law.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: the document contains no Issuer/Depositor indemnity running in favour of Cellco, so there is no customer-side indemnity to narrow. The mapping's citation of Section 9.2 is inapposite (it is a Depositor defence-of-title covenant in favour of the Issuer, not an indemnity of the Vendor), but the element is satisfied by absence and Section 9.2 was correctly left untouched.

elements.element: Vendor indemnifies Customer against third-party intellectual-property claims.
elements.evidence: Limb (C) of the new paragraph covers "any claim that any services or deliverables it provides under the Transaction Documents infringe or misappropriate any intellectual property right."

elements.element: The IP indemnity may exclude infringement caused by Customer modifications.
elements.evidence: Permissive element: no modification carve-out was inserted, which leaves the indemnity broader than the fallback tolerates and is therefore not a defect against Customer.

elements.element: The IP indemnity may exclude infringement caused by Customer combinations.
elements.evidence: Permissive element: no combination carve-out inserted; the unqualified limb (C) exceeds the fallback minimum in Customer's favour.

elements.element: The IP indemnity may exclude infringement caused by Customer specifications.
elements.evidence: Permissive element: no Customer-specification carve-out inserted; nothing narrows limb (C).

elements.element: Vendor must procure continued use, modify, or replace the infringing item.
elements.evidence: No procure/modify/replace remedy ladder appears anywhere in the rendered Section 6.3; the proposal deliberately omits it (only an indemnity, no corrective-remedy covenant).

elements.element: Vendor must refund applicable fees if procure, modify, or replace remedies are unavailable.
elements.evidence: No refund-of-fees fallback remedy is present in the rendered language; Section 6.3 speaks only to indemnification of losses.

elements.element: Vendor's indemnity is subject to a super-cap of three times annual fees.
elements.evidence: No cap language was added; the rendered Section 6.3 indemnity remains uncapped. Literally unmet, but the omission is Customer-favourable and the drafter states it was intentional.

elements.element: Vendor has an express duty to defend Customer and its affiliates.
elements.evidence: Duplicate-context check: the fallback checklist does not require a defence duty, and the operative text supplies one in any event ("will defend and indemnify").

reasons: Position-complete at the preferred level: every preferred element is met in operative text — mandatory "will defend and indemnify", extension to the Issuer's Affiliates, three new trigger limbs (violation of Law; unauthorized access to/disclosure of Obligor data or Receivable Files; third-party IP infringement/misappropriation of services or deliverables), retained notice and defence-control mechanics, and an added reasonable-cooperation sentence. The Customer-indemnity element is satisfied by absence: no Issuer or Depositor indemnity of Cellco exists, so there is nothing to narrow.

The fallback level is not complete (no procure/modify/replace ladder, no refund remedy, no 3x super-cap), but that is irrelevant because the preferred level is complete, and the missing super-cap and the missing IP carve-outs all leave the Customer better off than the fallback floor.

Minimality holds: the edits are confined to the four operative touchpoints needed to reach the preferred checklist. No favourable existing language was deleted (the permissive assumption-of-defence sentence, the non-prejudice notice proviso, the counsel-standard and separate-counsel/conflict provisions and the uncapped nature of the indemnity all survive), no survival tail, expense allocation, damages categories or boilerplate was imported, and the new limbs were drafted as a single sentence applying to both the Servicer and the Marketing Agent rather than duplicated in (a)(i) and (a)(ii).

Intent is preserved: the added cooperation sentence sits after the defence-assumption mechanics and does not contradict the retained permissive "may participate in and assume the defense" election; no cross-reference (Section 6.3(a), Section 6.7(b) of the Indenture, Section 7.2(a) of the Trust Agreement, which key off the "Indemnified Person" definition) is broken by widening the (a)(i) list, and Section 9.2 was correctly left intact.

Two definitional confirmations the drafter should make before sending, each fixable in the same sentence if wrong: (i) "Affiliates" as used in the new (a)(i) language must be a defined term in the Transaction Documents' definitions annex — if it is not, replace with the defined-term formulation or spell out "its affiliates" to avoid an undefined capitalized term; (ii) confirm "Law" and "Obligor" are likewise defined, since limb (A) and limb (B) rely on them.

Scope note on limb (B): the data-breach trigger is drafted to named categories ("Obligor data or Receivable Files") rather than to all data belonging to, supplied by or processed for the Issuer. That is defensible in a servicing/custodial context, but if the business wants belt-and-braces coverage, extend to "any Obligor data, Receivable Files or other information of or provided by the Issuer" — a one-phrase change that would not disturb minimality.

The rationale's suggestion that limb (C) could be dropped if there are no services/deliverables with IP subject matter should not be acted on: Cellco provides servicing and custodial services and systems under the Transaction Documents, and the detection guidance treats an indemnity without an IP limb as the deviation being cured. Dropping (C) would break the preferred level.
